$comment: Mid-century Modernism: principles and per-layer rules. The data lives beside this file: art.json (shape vocabulary, misregistration, texture, figure stylisation, palette ratios), motion.json (limited-animation timing), typography.json (type direction and fit), research.md (sources and reasoning). Colours always come from the colour system.
name: Mid-century Modernism
summary: Post-war graphic optimism, roughly 1945-1970: one emblematic image built from flat, cut-paper shapes, printed in two to four inks that sit slightly off register, with stylised birds, figures and atomic-age shapes (kidneys, boomerangs, starbursts). Modernist order underneath, American playfulness on top. Motion is limited animation: holds, stepped timing and title-sequence reveals.

principles.title: One emblem
principles.rule: Reduce the whole message to one emblematic image that a stranger could redraw from memory, as Saul Bass reduced a film to a cut-paper arm or a dismembered figure. One focal emblem per piece; everything else supports it.

principles.title: Cut, don't render
principles.rule: Build images from flat shapes with clean or scissor-cut edges, laid side by side or overlapping. No outlines needed; no modelling, gradients or shadows. Any texture comes from the printing (dry brush, speckle, halftone), never from lighting.
principles.source: Bass, Rand and Lustig cut-paper work (research.md 2.1-2.2)

principles.title: Off register, on purpose
principles.rule: Colour plates sit 0.75-1.5% of the short side away from the black key line, all in the same direction. The offset shows the work was printed in passes; it is fixed per piece, never random per shape.
principles.source: Limited-colour print practice (research.md 2.4; rule of thumb)

principles.title: Few inks
principles.rule: Two to four inks per piece, counting black; white is the unprinted paper. Colours sit next to each other and never mix: no overprint blends, no tints made with transparency.

principles.title: Count the wings
principles.rule: Stylise living things into 5-9 geometric parts drawn with ruler, compass and French curve: a bird is a body arc, a wedge tail, a triangle crest and a dot eye. Keep the one feature that makes it recognisable; drop the rest.

principles.title: Angular but friendly
principles.rule: Pair every sharp form (tapered triangle, starburst, boomerang tip) with a soft one (kidney, circle, arc). Sharp points cover at most a third of the outlines in a piece; corners on large shapes are rounded.
principles.source: Curvature preference (research.md 3) balanced against the period's angular vocabulary

principles.title: Play inside order
principles.rule: A clear modernist structure (grid, margins, left-aligned type, a strong hierarchy) with exactly one playful break: a tilted shape, a crop, a hand-drawn word or a figure stepping out of its frame.
principles.source: Swiss order and American New York School playfulness (research.md 2.3)

principles.title: Limited motion
principles.rule: Move like UPA cartoons and Bass titles: hold, then snap. Poses change on twos or threes (12 or 8 drawings a second), shapes cut on or slide in as bars, and one shape morphs into another. Every sequence ends on a held poster frame.
principles.source: UPA limited animation and Bass title sequences (research.md 2.1, 2.5)

layers.do: One Wada combination per piece, used as a 2-4 ink print job: its bg as the ground, one support colour for the big shape, the accent on the one emblem. Black key line (or the combination's own near-black ink when its light-mode inkUse is body). White is unprinted paper. Prefer warm grounds (ochre, orange-yellow, cream) against teal or turquoise, or the reverse (art.json palette).
layers.dont: More than four inks, overprint blends or transparency, gradients, shadows, glows, neon or metallic effects, large fields of muddy olive or brown with nothing bright beside them.

layers.do: A geometric or grotesque sans for headlines (heavy weight, tight spacing) with an old-style or Caslon-like serif for body and subheads, as rated in typography.json. Letter-spaced capitals for short labels. One or two words may be hand-lettered per piece if drawn for that piece.
layers.dont: Handwriting fonts, 'retro' novelty fonts used as body text, more than two families, script fonts in long lines, distressed fonts that fake wear.

layers.do: Asymmetric balance on a simple grid: 8% margins, one dominant emblem (40-70% of the short side), a left-aligned text block on the opposite side, a diagonal or a crop for energy. At least 35% empty ground.
layers.dont: Centred symmetrical stacks, filling every corner, frames and boxes around everything, more than one diagonal direction, text set over busy shape edges.

layers.do: Flat cut-paper shapes from the vocabulary in art.json (kidney, boomerang, starburst, leaf, tapered triangle, circle), stylised animals and figures built from 5-9 parts, a thin key line offset from the fills, light dry-brush or speckle texture on at most two shapes.
layers.dont: Realistic rendering, outlines traced exactly around fills, 3D, photo textures, Corporate Memphis figures, caricatures of ethnic groups or national costumes, pin-up or 'Mad Men' clichés.

layers.do: Limited animation: holds of 0.5-1.5 s between moves, poses stepped on twos (83 ms) or threes (125 ms), cut-on and bar-wipe reveals, a shape morphing into the next idea. Loops of 2-4 s ending on a held frame (motion.json).
layers.dont: Smooth 60 fps tweening of everything, camera moves and parallax, bouncy springs on text, constant motion with no holds, more than one thing moving at a time.

layers.do: Use sparingly. Photos cut out and set on a flat ground, converted to one ink (black or the combination's dark) as a coarse halftone, combined with drawn shapes, as Lustig and Rand did.
layers.dont: Full-colour glossy photos, vintage filters, fake film grain or scratches, sepia washes.

layers.do: Short, confident and a little witty, written to one person. Specific facts. The headline and image make one idea together; the image does not repeat the words.
layers.dont: Period pastiche ('Gee whiz', 'The modern housewife'), hype, exclamation marks, gendered 1950s stereotypes.

notes.curves: 1, not 2 as first estimated: kidneys, circles and arcs are curved, but boomerangs, starbursts, tapered triangles and Bass's jagged cut-outs are deliberately sharp. MC6 keeps points to a third of the outlines.
notes.simplicity: 2: one emblem, flat shapes and two to four inks are low in visual complexity, which is judged within 17-50 ms (simplicity finding).
notes.maya: 2: the look is familiar from decades of reuse yet still reads as fresh when the idea is new; the risk is pastiche, which tips it from 'advanced yet acceptable' into merely typical (maya finding).
notes.nature: 1: Harper's birds, leaves and suns bring nature in, but stylised to geometry; ruler-and-compass shapes are smoother than the mid-range fractal detail people prefer (fractals finding).
notes.handmade: 2, up from 1: cut edges, dry-brush skips, off-register colour and hand-lettered words are visible traces of hand and press, the kind of cue the handmade effect rests on (handmade finding).
notes.colour: 1: the period's ochres, olives and browns are among the least-liked colours on average; teal, turquoise, tomato red and cream are liked. Our palette method leans to the liked hues and keeps olive and brown to small areas (colour-valence finding).
notes.glance: 2: one silhouette on a flat contrasting ground reads before any words, as in the 50 ms first-impression studies (first-impression finding).

evidence.refinement: Same total as the original candidate rating (11/14) but a different shape: curves down from 2 to 1, handmade up from 1 to 2. The original rating underplayed the style's sharp atomic-age vocabulary and its print texture.

beyondPreference.note: When people's need to belong is active, they prefer nostalgic products (Loveland, Smeesters & Mandel 2010). Musical taste peaks for songs from one's late teens or early twenties (Holbrook & Schindler 1989; later replications move the peak younger). Mid-century imagery is 'second-hand' nostalgia for most audiences today, so the effect is weaker than for personal memories; treat it as a supporting reason, not the main one.
sources: Loveland, Smeesters & Mandel (2010), Journal of Consumer Research 37(3)
Holbrook & Schindler (1989), Journal of Consumer Research 16(1)

beyondPreference.note: A single emblem in a limited palette is easy to recall and redraw; Bass's Anatomy of a Murder figure and Golden Arm arm were reused across poster, titles and advertising as one recognisable mark. This is a design-history observation, not a measured effect.
sources: People's Graphic Design Archive, Anatomy of a Murder poster
BFI, Saul Bass's 10 essential title sequences

beyondPreference.note: The style carries post-war associations of optimism, modern living and good everyday design (Eames, Girard, Herman Miller). Useful for products that want to feel well made and democratic; a risk for products that must feel cutting-edge.
sources: Vitra, How Santa Fe shaped Alexander Girard
